It's the end of June. Mara has registered for the Goethe-Zertifikat B1 exam. The exam is in a week. In the evening, at Ludwig's, she has one last lesson.
Ludwig, I'm scared. The exam is in a week. What do I do if I fail?
You won't fail. You speak German better than half my neighbours. And they were born here.
You're saying that because you're kind. But the listening is hard. The people in the recordings speak so fast!
Then let's make a plan. Tomorrow you listen to the radio, for an hour. The day after tomorrow we watch the news together. And at the weekend you speak only German, even with Andrei on the phone.
With Andrei? He'll laugh at me!
He won't laugh. He's learning German too now, after all. Because of a certain baker.
Ha! That's true. All right. I'll study every day. I promise.
And what are you planning after the exam?
In August I'm going home for three weeks. Lena's coming too. Andrei will pick us up from the airport in Sibiu.
And then? Will you come back?
Ludwig! Of course I'll come back. My contract runs until next summer. And who else is going to sort out your phone problems?
That's true. Without you I'd have to write letters again. With stamps!
It'll be fine, Ludwig. It'll be fine.
“Prüfung” = “PRÜ-foong”: a long “ü”, and the final “ng” as in “sing”, with no separate “g”.
“Ergebnis” = “air-GAYP-nis”: g after r, and the b becomes a “p”.
“Zertifikat” = “tser-ti-fi-KAAT”: z = ts, stress at the end.
1. The future with the present tense
In German, you most often talk about the future with the PRESENT tense + a time expression. That's enough and it sounds the most natural:
Next week I'm taking the exam.
nächste Woche (f) / nächsten Monat (m) / nächstes Jahr (n)
“in zwei Wochen” = in two weeks' time (future). “vor zwei Wochen” = two weeks ago (past). “seit zwei Wochen” = for two weeks (still going on).
Conjugated “werden” in position 2, the infinitive at the END (as with modal verbs):
When do you use Futur I instead of the present? To EMPHASISE:
I will study every day. I promise. (promise, decision)

Careful: “werden” on its own = to become (chapter 14). “werden” + infinitive = future. “Ich werde Ärztin” = I'm becoming a doctor. “Ich werde arbeiten” = I will work. And don't confuse it with “will” (from wollen) = I want: “Ich will arbeiten” = I want to work!
“werden” + “wohl” (probably) + infinitive expresses a guess about the PRESENT:
Where's Ludwig? — He's probably at the doctor's.
Lena isn't answering. She's probably still asleep.
A very German expression of comfort: “Das wird schon!” = It'll be fine! / It'll work out!
das Ergebnis / die Note / die Punkte
the result / the mark / the points
The Goethe-Zertifikat B1 exam has four modules: Lesen (reading), Hören (listening), Schreiben (writing) and Sprechen (speaking). Each module can be passed separately; you need at least 60%.
“eine Prüfung machen” = to TAKE an exam (not to “make” it). “bestehen” = to pass. “Ich habe die Prüfung gemacht” doesn't say whether you passed!
Are you going to Italy in the summer?
What are you planning to do at the weekend?
Next week I'm going to Hamburg.
Wer wird Mara und Lena am Flughafen abholen?

The week before the exam was the longest week of Mara's life. She stuck to Ludwig's plan. Every morning she listened to the radio on the tram with her headphones on, and wrote down unknown words in a small green notebook. Every evening she watched the eight o'clock news with Ludwig, and afterwards she had to tell him what she had understood. At first it wasn't much. By Friday it was almost everything.

On Saturday she spoke only German. With Lena at the bakery, with the twins on the stairs, with Mrs Hoffmann over tea. On Sunday she rang Andrei. He answered in German, slowly, with lots of mistakes, but with an accent he had clearly got from Lena: he said “icke” instead of “ich”. Mara laughed so hard she almost fell off the sofa.

The night before the exam she couldn't sleep. At midnight she was still lying awake, thinking: “What will I do if I don't manage the listening? What will I tell Mum? What will Ludwig think?” At one o'clock she got up and made herself a tea. On the kitchen table lay a note that someone had slipped under her door. On it, in big, shaky letters, was written:

“Dear Mara, tomorrow you won't be perfect. Nobody is perfect. But you'll be good. And if not, then you will be next time. It'll be fine. Good luck! Yours, Ludwig. PS: Fritz is keeping his paws crossed for you, all four of them.”
Mara put the note under her pillow, like a child, and fell asleep at once.

The exam took place at the Goethe-Institut, in a modern building in Mitte. In the waiting room sat twenty people from all over the world: a doctor from Syria, a young cook from Vietnam, a couple from Brazil, two students from Spain. They all looked just as nervous as Mara. The cook from Vietnam smiled at her and whispered: “We'll make it.” Mara smiled back.

The reading went well. The texts were about topics she knew: an article about neighbours helping each other in big cities, an email from a friend, the rules of a swimming pool. Mara almost laughed when she read the article. “Neighbours help neighbours,” it said. “In many buildings people don't know each other any more.” She thought of Kastanienallee and thought: “In my building they do.”

Then came the listening. The first recording was an announcement at a station, fast and with lots of background noise. Mara understood only half. Her heart was pounding. But then she heard Ludwig's voice in her head: “Not every word, Mara. The main point. What's the main point?” She took a deep breath and listened a second time. The train to Hamburg was delayed. Platform seven instead of platform three. That was the main point.

In the break she ate an apple and read Ludwig's note once more; she had secretly slipped it into her bag. Rana, the doctor from Syria, sat down next to her and told her that in Damascus she had worked as a paediatrician for twenty years. In Germany she wasn't allowed to work yet, because she first had to pass the language exam. “Next year I'll be treating children again,” she said calmly. “I know that.” Mara thought that her own worries suddenly seemed much smaller.

For the writing she had to write an email to a friend and talk about her plans for the summer. Mara smiled. She wrote about Sibiu, about the trip with Lena, about her brother, who would pick her up from the airport, and about an old man with a yellow lamp who had taught her German. She wrote six lines more than she needed to.

In the afternoon came the speaking test. Her partner was Rana, the calm doctor from Syria, who had been living in Berlin for a year. Together they had to plan a farewell party for a colleague. When? Where? Who brings what? Rana suggested a restaurant. Mara suggested a courtyard, with fairy lights and music from an open window. The examiner, an older woman with red glasses, raised her eyebrows and made a note.
That's a very nice idea, Ms Ionescu. Where did you get it from?
From my life, to be honest.

When Mara came out of the building at five, she was as tired as after a night shift. In front of the entrance, on a bench in the sun, sat two familiar figures. Ludwig, with his hat, and next to him Lena, with a white box on her lap. Fritz was lying at their feet, asleep.
I don't know. The result comes in four weeks. Maybe I'll pass. Maybe not.
You'll pass. And until then we'll eat cake. I've baked you a plum cake. For your nerves.

The three of them sat down on the bench in the warm July sun and ate the cake with their hands, no plates, no forks. A few tourists walked past and looked at them curiously: a young woman, a baker with flour on her apron, an old man in a hat and a sleeping dachshund. Mara thought that at that moment she didn't know whether she had passed the exam. But she knew she wasn't alone. And that, as Ludwig would have said, was the main point.
